title: Game Theory and Cooperation
description: A university lecture, a seminar discussion, a radio essay and an academic debate about why people cooperate and what game theory can tell us.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · The puzzle of cooperation
parts.intro: You will hear the opening of a university lecture on game theory.

script.speaker: Dr Pryce
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to begin with a puzzle that has troubled economists, biologists and philosophers for the better part of a century: why do rational individuals ever cooperate?

script.speaker: Dr Pryce
script.text: The classic illustration is the prisoner's dilemma. Two suspects are held in separate rooms. If both stay silent, each serves one year. If one betrays the other, the betrayer walks free and the silent partner serves ten. If both betray, they each serve five.

script.speaker: Dr Pryce
script.text: Now, the logic is rather unsettling. Whatever your partner does, you are better off betraying. So both of you betray, and both serve five years, when mutual silence would have cost only one.

script.speaker: Dr Pryce
script.text: I should stress that this is not a story about stupidity. Each prisoner reasons perfectly well. The trouble is that individually sensible choices add up to a collectively poor outcome.

script.speaker: Dr Pryce
script.text: Early researchers, I'm told, found this result almost offensive. They assumed that cooperation, which we see everywhere in daily life, must be explained by kindness or moral instinct. But the mathematics suggested otherwise, and that is what makes the field so fascinating.

script.speaker: Dr Pryce
script.text: Actually, I'd go further. The real puzzle is not why cooperation fails in a single encounter, but why it so often succeeds when people meet again and again. We will come to that shortly, but first let me make clear what the model assumes, because the assumptions matter.

script.speaker: Dr Pryce
script.text: It assumes the players cannot talk, cannot make binding promises, and care only about their own sentence. Relax any of those, and the dilemma begins to dissolve. Which, of course, is rather the point.

parts.title: Part 2 · A seminar on repeated games
parts.intro: You will hear a student, Linh, asking Professor Hale about repeated games.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: Professor Hale, may I ask something about the repeated version? If the game goes on indefinitely, surely cooperation just becomes obviously rational?

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: Not obviously, Linh, but often, yes. Back in the nineteen-eighties a political scientist ran a famous tournament, inviting experts to submit strategies for a repeated dilemma and then pitting them against one another by computer.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: Many entries were fiendishly clever. Some tried to detect patterns in the opponent's behaviour and exploit them. The winner, however, was the simplest of all, a strategy called tit for tat, only four lines long.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: What did it actually do?

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: It cooperated on the first move, and from then on simply copied whatever the other player had done the previous time. Betray it once, and it betrays you once. Forgive, and it forgives.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: So it was nice, but not a pushover.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: Precisely. The researcher drew four lessons: be nice, meaning never betray first; be retaliatory; be forgiving; and be clear, so your opponent can predict you. Interestingly, the strategies that tried to be too clever tended to confuse their opponents and provoke endless feuds.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: But in real life we never know when a relationship will end. Doesn't that change things?

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: A sharp point. The theory depends on what's called the shadow of the future. If you believe you'll meet again, the future casts a shadow over today's temptation. If the final round is known, cooperation unravels from the end backwards: no one cooperates in the last round, so the second-to-last is effectively last, and so on.

script.speaker: Linh
script.text: That seems almost too pessimistic.

script.speaker: Professor Hale
script.text: It does, and experiments bear you out. Real people cooperate for longer than the theory predicts, although they do tend to defect as the final round approaches. I'd say that is a useful reminder that models are maps, not territories.

parts.title: Part 3 · The tragedy of the commons
parts.intro: You will hear a radio essay about shared resources.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Every autumn, in the village I grew up in, there was an argument about the common pasture. Nobody owned it, everybody could graze their sheep on it, and everybody agreed it was looking tired.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Years later I discovered that this small quarrel has a grand name, the tragedy of the commons, coined by an ecologist who argued that shared resources are doomed. Each herder gains the full benefit of one more animal, but shares the cost of overgrazing with everybody else. So each adds another sheep, and the pasture collapses.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: For decades, this was treated as an iron law. The proposed remedies were stark: either hand the pasture to private owners, or let the state take charge and police it.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Then a political economist, who would eventually win the Nobel prize, did something unfashionable. She went and looked. She studied fisheries, forests and irrigation systems across the world, and found countless communities that had managed shared resources sensibly for centuries, with neither privatisation nor a distant government.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: What they had in common was not saintliness. They had clear boundaries about who could use the resource. They agreed their own rules, monitored one another, and applied modest penalties that grew with repeated offences. Disputes were settled cheaply and locally.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I find this strangely moving, though I realise sentimentality is a poor guide. The lesson is not that people are naturally good. It is that goodness is cheaper to sustain when the arrangements make cheating visible and unrewarding.

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Which brings me back to my village. The pasture, as it happens, was rescued by a grazing rota drawn up by two stubborn neighbours who disliked each other intensely. Nobody was kind. They simply wrote everything down.

parts.title: Part 4 · Does game theory describe real life?
parts.intro: You will hear two academics, Dr Mai and Dr Bennett, discussing the value of game theory.

script.speaker: Dr Mai
script.text: Let me play devil's advocate. Game theory is elegant, but I worry that we sell it as a guide to real life when it's really a study of toy situations.

script.speaker: Dr Bennett
script.text: I'd resist that, Mai. A toy model isn't useless because it's simple. A wind tunnel doesn't look like the sky either, but nobody builds aircraft without one.

script.speaker: Dr Mai
script.text: Fair, but aircraft engineers test their models against reality. Take climate negotiations. Commentators love to call them a prisoner's dilemma, and conclude that failure is inevitable. Yet countries have cut some pollutants dramatically, for example the chemicals that damaged the ozone layer.

script.speaker: Dr Bennett
script.text: Which is a good counter-example, but it's also instructive. That treaty worked because the substitutes were cheap, trade penalties applied to outsiders, and everyone could verify compliance. In other words, the game was changed, not ignored.

script.speaker: Dr Mai
script.text: So you'd say the discipline's real value is in redesigning the game?

script.speaker: Dr Bennett
script.text: Largely, yes. Telling people to be nicer rarely works. Changing incentives, as with the grazing rota, often does. Mechanism design, as we call it, asks: if I want cooperation, what rules would make it each person's best move?

script.speaker: Dr Mai
script.text: My concern is that it treats people as calculators. Humans care about fairness. In experiments, people reject offers they consider insulting, even at a cost to themselves.

script.speaker: Dr Bennett
script.text: Agreed, and the better modern work builds that in. Preferences for fairness are simply another term in the equation, not an embarrassment to the theory.

script.speaker: Dr Mai
script.text: Then we're closer than I expected. Perhaps my quarrel is with popular summaries rather than the science.

script.speaker: Dr Bennett
script.text: I suspect so. The danger is anyone who says the theory proves cooperation is impossible. It has never shown that. It shows when cooperation needs help.

questions.text: What is the lecturer's main aim in this opening section?
options: To raise the question of why self-interested people cooperate
To argue that prisoners behave irrationally when under pressure
To describe how criminal sentences are decided in court
To prove that kindness explains cooperation in daily life
questions.explanation: She opens with the puzzle of why rational individuals cooperate and then explains the prisoner's dilemma as an illustration.

evidence.quote: why do rational individuals ever cooperate?

questions.text: In the prisoner's dilemma, what happens if both suspects betray each other?
options: Each serves only one year
Each serves ten years in prison
Each serves five years
One goes free
questions.explanation: The lecturer says that if both betray, they each serve five years. One year is for mutual silence and ten is for the silent partner.

evidence.quote: If both betray, they each serve five.

questions.text: What does the lecturer imply about the prisoners' reasoning?
options: It is sound and leads them to the best joint outcome
It is sound, yet it produces a poor result for both
It is flawed because they lack information about each other
It is driven mainly by moral instinct rather than logic
questions.explanation: She says each prisoner reasons perfectly well, but sensible individual choices add up to a poor collective outcome.

evidence.quote: individually sensible choices add up to a collectively poor outcome

questions.text: The lecturer suggests that the early researchers' reaction to the result was
options: justified by errors in the mathematics
unimportant for the development of the field
a sign of how surprising the mathematics was
proof that kindness explains cooperation
questions.explanation: The researchers found the result almost offensive, and the lecturer says the mathematics is what makes the field fascinating.

evidence.quote: found this result almost offensive

questions.text: Why does the lecturer list the assumptions of the model at the end?
options: To move on to a quite unrelated subject
To show that changing them can alter the outcome
To suggest that the model is of no real use
To apologise for oversimplifying the topic so much
questions.explanation: She says that if any assumption is relaxed, the dilemma begins to dissolve, which is the point of mentioning them.

evidence.quote: Relax any of those, and the dilemma begins to dissolve.

questions.text: What was surprising about the winner of the tournament?
options: It always betrayed first
It was written by the most experienced entrant
It detected the opponent's patterns
It was extremely simple
questions.explanation: The professor says many entries were clever, but the winner was the simplest of all, only four lines long.

evidence.quote: the simplest of all

questions.text: How did tit for tat behave after its first move?
options: It cooperated whatever the opponent did
It repeated the other player's previous move
It alternated between cooperating and betraying
It punished any betrayal permanently
questions.explanation: After cooperating first, it copied what the other player had done the time before, so it could forgive as well as retaliate.

evidence.quote: simply copied whatever the other player had done the previous time

questions.text: Why did the overly clever strategies perform badly?
options: They were too forgiving of betrayal by opponents
Opponents could not read them, which provoked feuds
They cooperated too readily with everyone they met
They took too long to calculate each of their moves
questions.explanation: The professor says clever strategies confused opponents and provoked endless feuds, so they were not clear or predictable.

evidence.quote: tended to confuse their opponents and provoke endless feuds

questions.text: Why does Professor Hale mention the shadow of the future?
options: To criticise the way the tournament had been designed
To suggest that people ignore what happens later on
To explain why expecting to meet again encourages cooperation
To argue that known endings make people more generous
questions.explanation: In answer to Linh's question about uncertain endings, he explains that believing you will meet again discourages betrayal today.

evidence.quote: If you believe you'll meet again, the future casts a shadow over today's temptation.

questions.text: What is Professor Hale's attitude to the theory's pessimistic prediction?
options: He is embarrassed that the theory sounds so negative about people
He accepts it simplifies reality and experiments partly contradict it
He believes it describes real behaviour accurately in experiments
He dismisses the experiments as unreliable and too small to matter
questions.explanation: He agrees with Linh, notes that real people cooperate longer than predicted, and calls models maps, not territories.

evidence.quote: models are maps, not territories

questions.text: According to the essay, why does each herder add another animal?
options: He believes the pasture is so large that it can never run out
He gets the whole benefit but shares the cost with others
He wants to damage the flocks of the other herders
He has been ordered to add more animals by the state
questions.explanation: The speaker explains that each herder gains the full benefit of one more animal but shares the cost of overgrazing.

evidence.quote: Each herder gains the full benefit of one more animal

questions.text: What does the speaker imply about the iron law view of shared resources?
options: It was accepted before being checked against real cases
It was based on extensive fieldwork in many countries
It was never taken seriously by experts in the field
It was invented by a government to justify its control
questions.explanation: He says it was treated as an iron law for decades until the political economist went and looked at actual communities.

evidence.quote: She went and looked.

questions.text: What did the successful communities have in common?
options: Unusually generous and saintly members who put others first
Clear boundaries and their own rules with graduated penalties
A strong central authority that policed the resource closely
Private ownership of the resource by each separate family
questions.explanation: They defined who could use the resource, agreed their own rules and applied modest penalties that grew with repeated offences.

evidence.quote: They had clear boundaries about who could use the resource.

questions.text: How does the speaker feel about the political economist's findings?
options: Indifferent to their importance for ordinary people
Doubtful that they apply to the modern world at all
Moved by them, but wary of letting sentiment guide him
Convinced that people are naturally good, if given the chance
questions.explanation: He finds them strangely moving but admits sentimentality is a poor guide, and says the lesson is not that people are naturally good.

evidence.quote: I find this strangely moving, though I realise sentimentality is a poor guide.

questions.text: Why does the speaker end with the story of his village?
options: To suggest that the state should have stepped in
To show that clear arrangements, not kindness, solved it
To complain about his stubborn former neighbours
To show that rivals cooperate less often than friends
questions.explanation: The pasture was saved by a rota written by two neighbours who disliked each other, so kindness played no part.

evidence.quote: Nobody was kind. They simply wrote everything down.

questions.text: What is Dr Mai's initial concern about game theory?
options: It is far too difficult for most students to learn well
It is presented as a guide to real life but studies simple cases
It cannot be tested by computers or by experiments
It ignores the earlier work of biologists and ecologists
questions.explanation: She says it is sold as a guide to real life when it is really a study of toy situations.

evidence.quote: we sell it as a guide to real life when it's really a study of toy situations

questions.text: Why does Dr Bennett mention a wind tunnel?
options: To show that engineers distrust their own models
To explain how climate treaties are usually tested
To argue that a simple model can still be valuable
To criticise the growing use of computers in research work
questions.explanation: He compares a toy model to a wind tunnel, which does not look like the sky but is still essential for building aircraft.

evidence.quote: A wind tunnel doesn't look like the sky either, but nobody builds aircraft without one.

questions.text: What does Dr Bennett's account of the ozone treaty suggest?
options: The prisoner's dilemma does not exist in politics
Cooperation succeeded because the conditions were changed
Countries cooperate naturally without any incentives
The treaty worked despite cheap substitutes being unavailable
questions.explanation: He says the treaty worked because of cheap substitutes, penalties for outsiders and verification, so the game was changed.

evidence.quote: the game was changed, not ignored

questions.text: According to Dr Bennett, what does mechanism design ask?
options: How people can be persuaded to become kinder to others
How to prove that cooperation is impossible in practice
What rules would make cooperation each person's best move
How to remove all incentives from a situation
questions.explanation: He defines it as asking which rules would make cooperation each person's best move.

evidence.quote: what rules would make it each person's best move?

questions.text: How do the speakers' views compare by the end of the discussion?
options: They still disagree completely about whether fairness matters
They broadly agree; Dr Mai's complaint is about popular summaries
Dr Bennett accepts that the theory is useless in practice
Dr Mai believes that cooperation is impossible without a state
questions.explanation: Dr Mai says they are closer than expected and that her quarrel is with popular summaries, and Dr Bennett agrees.

evidence.quote: Perhaps my quarrel is with popular summaries rather than the science.
